arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm2.prompt_text:
You will be shown SEVERAL images of one solid block built from interlocking
cube pieces. They arrive in a fixed order:

  the first six    the six surface views, in the order +X, +Y, +Z, -X, -Y, -Z
  then             every remaining image shows ONE piece by itself, in letter
                   order A, B, C, ... from a first angle, then the same pieces
                   again in the same letter order from a second angle

Every cell of a surface view is labelled with the letter of the piece it exposes,
and every piece image is badged with its letter. Each piece image is also
captioned with the exact number of cubes that piece contains, its bounding box,
and which of the six face directions that view exposes. The cube count is exact
and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face
directions, so no outer face of a piece is hidden across the pair — but cubes
sitting fully inside a piece are visible in neither view, and the cube count is
how you account for them.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm2.prompt_text:
You will be shown SEVERAL images of one solid block built from interlocking
cube pieces. They arrive in a fixed order:

  the first six    the six surface views, in the order +X, +Y, +Z, -X, -Y, -Z
  then             every remaining image shows ONE piece by itself, in letter
                   order A, B, C, ... from a first angle, then the same pieces
                   again in the same letter order from a second angle

Every cell of a surface view is labelled with the letter of the piece it exposes,
and every piece image is badged with its letter. Each piece image is also
captioned with the exact number of cubes that piece contains, its bounding box,
and which of the six face directions that view exposes. The cube count is exact
and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face
directions, so no outer face of a piece is hidden across the pair — but cubes
sitting fully inside a piece are visible in neither view, and the cube count is
how you account for them.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face

how you account for them.

along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

work out what the withheld view must look like.

     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as

     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm2.prompt_text:
You will be shown SEVERAL images of one solid block built from interlocking
cube pieces. They arrive in a fixed order:

  the first six    the six surface views, in the order +X, +Y, +Z, -X, -Y, -Z
  then             every remaining image shows ONE piece by itself, in letter
                   order A, B, C, ... from a first angle, then the same pieces
                   again in the same letter order from a second angle

Every cell of a surface view is labelled with the letter of the piece it exposes,
and every piece image is badged with its letter. Each piece image is also
captioned with the exact number of cubes that piece contains, its bounding box,
and which of the six face directions that view exposes. The cube count is exact
and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face
directions, so no outer face of a piece is hidden across the pair — but cubes
sitting fully inside a piece are visible in neither view, and the cube count is
how you account for them.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm2.prompt_text:
You will be shown SEVERAL images of one solid block built from interlocking
cube pieces. They arrive in a fixed order:

  the first six    the six surface views, in the order +X, +Y, +Z, -X, -Y, -Z
  then             every remaining image shows ONE piece by itself, in letter
                   order A, B, C, ... from a first angle, then the same pieces
                   again in the same letter order from a second angle

Every cell of a surface view is labelled with the letter of the piece it exposes,
and every piece image is badged with its letter. Each piece image is also
captioned with the exact number of cubes that piece contains, its bounding box,
and which of the six face directions that view exposes. The cube count is exact
and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face
directions, so no outer face of a piece is hidden across the pair — but cubes
sitting fully inside a piece are visible in neither view, and the cube count is
how you account for them.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm2.prompt_text:
You will be shown SEVERAL images of one solid block built from interlocking
cube pieces. They arrive in a fixed order:

  the first six    the six surface views, in the order +X, +Y, +Z, -X, -Y, -Z
  then             every remaining image shows ONE piece by itself, in letter
                   order A, B, C, ... from a first angle, then the same pieces
                   again in the same letter order from a second angle

Every cell of a surface view is labelled with the letter of the piece it exposes,
and every piece image is badged with its letter. Each piece image is also
captioned with the exact number of cubes that piece contains, its bounding box,
and which of the six face directions that view exposes. The cube count is exact
and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face
directions, so no outer face of a piece is hidden across the pair — but cubes
sitting fully inside a piece are visible in neither view, and the cube count is
how you account for them.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

You will be shown SEVERAL images of one solid block built from interlocking
cube pieces. They arrive in a fixed order:

  the first six    the six surface views, in the order +X, +Y, +Z, -X, -Y, -Z
  then             every remaining image shows ONE piece by itself, in letter
                   order A, B, C, ... from a first angle, then the same pieces
                   again in the same letter order from a second angle

Every cell of a surface view is labelled with the letter of the piece it exposes,
and every piece image is badged with its letter. Each piece image is also
captioned with the exact number of cubes that piece contains, its bounding box,
and which of the six face directions that view exposes. The cube count is exact
and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face
directions, so no outer face of a piece is hidden across the pair — but cubes
sitting fully inside a piece are visible in neither view, and the cube count is
how you account for them.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels

  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm2.prompt_text:
You will be shown SEVERAL images of one solid block built from interlocking
cube pieces. They arrive in a fixed order:

  the first six    the six surface views, in the order +X, +Y, +Z, -X, -Y, -Z
  then             every remaining image shows ONE piece by itself, in letter
                   order A, B, C, ... from a first angle, then the same pieces
                   again in the same letter order from a second angle

Every cell of a surface view is labelled with the letter of the piece it exposes,
and every piece image is badged with its letter. Each piece image is also
captioned with the exact number of cubes that piece contains, its bounding box,
and which of the six face directions that view exposes. The cube count is exact
and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face
directions, so no outer face of a piece is hidden across the pair — but cubes
sitting fully inside a piece are visible in neither view, and the cube count is
how you account for them.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm2.prompt_text:
You will be shown SEVERAL images of one solid block built from interlocking
cube pieces. They arrive in a fixed order:

  the first six    the six surface views, in the order +X, +Y, +Z, -X, -Y, -Z
  then             every remaining image shows ONE piece by itself, in letter
                   order A, B, C, ... from a first angle, then the same pieces
                   again in the same letter order from a second angle

Every cell of a surface view is labelled with the letter of the piece it exposes,
and every piece image is badged with its letter. Each piece image is also
captioned with the exact number of cubes that piece contains, its bounding box,
and which of the six face directions that view exposes. The cube count is exact
and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face
directions, so no outer face of a piece is hidden across the pair — but cubes
sitting fully inside a piece are visible in neither view, and the cube count is
how you account for them.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm2.prompt_text:
You will be shown SEVERAL images of one solid block built from interlocking
cube pieces. They arrive in a fixed order:

  the first six    the six surface views, in the order +X, +Y, +Z, -X, -Y, -Z
  then             every remaining image shows ONE piece by itself, in letter
                   order A, B, C, ... from a first angle, then the same pieces
                   again in the same letter order from a second angle

Every cell of a surface view is labelled with the letter of the piece it exposes,
and every piece image is badged with its letter. Each piece image is also
captioned with the exact number of cubes that piece contains, its bounding box,
and which of the six face directions that view exposes. The cube count is exact
and you should use it: any reading of a piece that does not have exactly that
many cubes is wrong. The two views of each piece together expose all six face
directions, so no outer face of a piece is hidden across the pair — but cubes
sitting fully inside a piece are visible in neither view, and the cube count is
how you account for them.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.

arm4.prompt_text:
You will be shown one image of a solid block built from interlocking cube pieces,
laid out as a single sheet: a top row of the six surface views, and below it the
same pieces pulled apart from two angles.

Each piece is a different color, and the legend at the top right of the image
maps every color to a letter.

THE SURFACE VIEWS
Each is a square grid, and every cell records exactly what that face exposes
along that line of sight:

  * a solid colored cell — the ray hits that piece right at the surface
  * a smaller, darker colored cell inset in grey — recessed: the ray travels
    down a channel into the block before hitting that piece
  * a plain light-grey cell — a hole straight through the block; nothing is hit

Five of the six are drawn. The sixth is not: in its place is a dashed red grid
containing "?" and labelled "VIEW <axis> — PREDICT THIS". That is your target.

READ THE CAPTIONS — they carry information you need and are always correct.
Each surface panel is captioned "VIEW <axis>" with that panel's own screen axes,
written "-> <right>   ^ <up>". Each face has its OWN axes; they differ from face
to face and cannot all be the same.

THE PIECES
Each piece is shown alone, from two angles, giving its complete 3D shape. On some
items the pieces are shown ROTATED — turned into a different orientation from the
one they occupy in the block — so you may have to work out each piece's rotation
as well as its position. Only proper rotations are used, never mirror images.

YOUR TASK
Reconstruct the block from the five given views and the piece views, then
work out what the withheld view must look like.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS — do not mix them up

  1. WORKING OUT the hidden face needs the axes. The caption under each panel
     says which way its two screen directions point in the block, written as
     arrows: "→ -Y  ↑ +Z" means that as you move right across that panel you
     are moving in -Y, and as you move up you are moving in +Z. Use this to
     reason about how the views relate to each other in 3D.

  2. WRITING the answer needs no axes at all. Just read the "PREDICT THIS"
     panel the way you read anything: top row first, then downward; within a
     row, leftmost character first, then rightward. Its rows and columns are
     numbered 1..N in the picture — write them in that order.

OUTPUT
The "PREDICT THIS" panel has the same number of rows and columns as the five
views that are drawn. Reply with a JSON object containing exactly two keys:

  {
    "reason": "brief account of how you worked it out",
    "answer": ["DDDDD", ".DDDB", "DDAAB", "DDCAC", "ADCCC"]
  }

  * "answer" is an array of strings, ONE STRING PER ROW, top to bottom. The
    first string is the panel's row 1 (the top row); the last is its bottom row.
  * WITHIN A STRING, one character per column, left to right. The first
    character is column 1 (the leftmost); the last is the rightmost.
  * use the piece's LETTER where that piece is the first thing the ray meets
  * use "." for a cell you can see straight through
  * every string is the same length, and there are as many strings as there are
    characters in each one. The example above is 5x5 because it is only an
    example — match whatever size the panel actually is, and note that its
    letters mean nothing.
  * "reason" is free text, recorded but not scored. Write as much or as little
    as you need.

No prose outside the object, no code fence, no trailing commentary — just the
JSON object.

ANSWER FORMAT — output exactly this shape and nothing else:

{"reason": "row 3 is B because the +Y view shows B nearest along that ray",
 "answer": ["BBBB", "BBBC", "AA.C", "CCCC"]}

Same idea at whatever size the panel is: one string per row, top row first.
